[3] (document: 02_Materials_Coatings_and_Weldability.docx | section: 1. What "Weldability" Formally Means)
ISO 18278-1 supplies the formal framework this reference set uses for the word "weldability." It specifies procedures for assessing the generic weldability for resistance welding of uncoated and coated metals, and it does so for four distinct purposes: comparing metallurgical weldability across different metals, assessing the weldability of varying component designs, investigating the effect of changing welding parameters, and comparing the performance of different resistance-welding equipment [S10]. That four-purpose scope is worth reading carefully, because it means "weldability" is never a single yes/no property of a material sample sitting on a bench — it is always a statement relative to a design, a parameter set, or a piece of equipment as well as to the metal itself.

[2] (document: 03_Electrodes_and_Tooling.docx | section: 6. Tip-Dressing Equipment and Procedure)
Tip dressing removes a controlled amount of material from the electrode face to restore a specified face geometry. The equipment used to do this — the tip dresser — is a rotary cutter or abrasive dressing head, mechanically integrated into many production cells so that dressing can occur in place on the gun without removing the electrode, though standalone bench-mounted dressers are also in service. Whichever form it takes, the tip dresser's function is the same: to remove a controlled, repeatable amount of material from the tip face and restore a defined target profile (dome, truncated cone, flat, or whatever geometry the design calls for), not simply to "clean up" the tip by eye.

QUESTION: Why is tip dressing not simply about cleaning up the tip by eye?
Tip dressing removes a controlled amount of material from the electrode face to restore a specified face geometry, not simply to 'clean up' the tip by eye. [2]

Group 9 covers brazing, soldering and braze welding. These are distinct from welding by definition: the parent metal is not melted, and the joint is made by a filler that melts below the parent's melting range and is distributed by capillary action (in brazing and soldering) or deposited like a weld bead without parent fusion (in braze welding). The dividing line between brazing and soldering is conventionally the 450 °C liquidus of the filler — above it is brazing, below it is soldering. Chapters 66 through 68 cover the family and, more usefully, cover when to recommend it instead of welding.

The sonotrode and anvil faces are patterned — knurled, serrated or textured — and this is functional rather than cosmetic:

3. The Weld Types

Groove welds fill a prepared gap between members. The preparation shapes are: square (no preparation, thin material only), single and double V, single and double bevel, single and double U, single and double J, and the flare grooves (flare-V and flare-bevel) formed by the natural radius between curved members such as tube-to-plate.

Groove welds are either complete joint penetration (CJP), where the weld extends fully through the joint thickness, or partial joint penetration (PJP), where it deliberately does not. Traceability is the ability to connect a completed weld to the conditions under which it was made. The elements normally required:

• Which parent material heat or cast the joint was made in.

• What heat treatment the joint received, and the record of that cycle.

• What inspection was performed, by whom, and with what result.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 Reference 442

Magnetic pulse welding discharges a large stored electrical charge through a coil placed around or beside a workpiece. The resulting intense, rapidly changing magnetic field induces opposing currents in the workpiece, and the interaction between the field and those induced currents produces a repulsive force that accelerates the workpiece across a small gap onto a mating part. The two collide at high velocity and weld in the solid state.

The ISO nomenclature lists it as reference 442, magnetic pulse welding, immediately after 441, explosion welding [S1] — and that adjacency is metallurgically correct: both are high-velocity impact welding processes, differing only in how the flyer is accelerated.

The whole event takes tens of microseconds. There is no heat

The distribution of actual harm is not the distribution of perceived risk, and this is worth stating plainly at the outset:

• Burns and eye injuries are the most frequent injuries, and are mostly minor to moderate.

• Fume exposure causes the greatest total burden of serious harm, but the harm is chronic and delayed, so it is systematically under-perceived by the people exposed.

Welders and engineers who arrive at aluminium from a steel background consistently underestimate it, and the reason is that aluminium violates the sensory cues that steel practice is built on.

It does not change colour before it melts. Steel glows through a predictable sequence and an experienced welder reads heat from it. Aluminium goes from solid to collapsed with no visual warning, which is why unsupported thin aluminium falls out of the joint so readily.

Tip dressing removes a controlled amount of material from the electrode face to restore a specified face geometry. The equipment used to do this — the tip dresser — is a rotary cutter or abrasive dressing head, mechanically integrated into many production cells so that dressing can occur in place on the gun without removing the electrode, though standalone bench-mounted dressers are also in service. Welders and engineers who arrive at aluminium from a steel background consistently underestimate it, and the reason is that aluminium violates the sensory cues that steel practice is built on.

It does not change colour before it melts. Steel glows through a predictable sequence and an experienced welder reads heat from it. Aluminium goes from solid to collapsed with no visual warning, which is why unsupported thin aluminium falls out of the joint so readily.

Its thermal conductivity is roughly four to six times that of steel. Heat runs out of the joint immediately. This produces the counter-intuitive result that aluminium generally requires higher current than steel of the same thickness despite melting at less than half the temperature — the heat source is competing with a far more effective heat sink. 8. Shielding Gas and Plume Control

Shielding gas does two jobs in laser welding, and the second has no equivalent in arc welding:

Protecting the pool from oxidation, as in any fusion process.

Controlling the vapour plume. Metal vapour above the keyhole absorbs and scatters the beam. At the CO₂ wavelength this is severe enough to require active suppression; at near-infrared wavelengths it is milder but still present at high power.

Gas selection reflects both jobs: helium has a high ionization potential and suppresses plume formation effectively, and is the traditional choice for CO₂ laser welding despite its cost. 3. Why It Is Explosion Welding by Another Driver

The physics from the collision onward is identical to explosion welding (Chapter 59), and the same three features appear:

Jetting cleans the interface. No surface preparation to metallurgical cleanliness is required, because the jet removes the surface layers of both parts at the moment of impact.

The bond line is characteristically wavy. A properly made magnetic pulse weld shows the same periodic wave pattern in cross-section, and the same diagnostic reading applies: regular waves indicate a weld made inside the window; a flat interface indicates the low-energy edge; melted pockets at wave vortices indicate excessive energy.

8. Shielding Gas and Plume Control

Shielding gas does two jobs in laser welding, and the second has no equivalent in arc welding:

Protecting the pool from oxidation, as in any fusion process.

Controlling the vapour plume. Metal vapour above the keyhole absorbs and scatters the beam. At the CO₂ wavelength this is severe enough to require active suppression; at near-infrared wavelengths it is milder but still present at high power.

Gas selection reflects both jobs: helium has a high ionization potential and suppresses plume formation effectively, and is the traditional choice for CO₂ laser welding despite its cost. 5. Hydrogen Porosity: The Characteristic Aluminium Defect

Hydrogen is highly soluble in molten aluminium and almost insoluble in solid aluminium. During solidification the dissolved hydrogen is rejected from the advancing solid, becomes supersaturated in the remaining liquid, and forms bubbles. If the pool solidifies before the bubbles escape, they are trapped as porosity.

This mechanism is unavoidable in principle and controllable in practice. Sources of hydrogen:

• Moisture in the oxide film on the parent metal or on the filler wire — the largest single source in most shops.

• Hydrocarbons: oil, grease, cutting fluid, drawing lubricant residue on filler wire, fingerprints.

The physics from the collision onward is identical to explosion welding (Chapter 59), and the same three features appear:

10. The Fit-Up Problem

This is the process's defining practical limitation, and it decides more laser welding projects than any metallurgical consideration.

The mechanism. A focused beam may be a few tenths of a millimetre across. A butt joint with a gap wider than the beam presents nothing for the beam to strike — it passes through, melting the edges inadequately or not at all. There is no filler being added and no wide arc cone to bridge the gap, so the process cannot compensate for a gap the way any arc process can.

The consequences:

• Fit-up tolerances are far tighter than for arc welding — typically a small fraction of the material thickness, and often st

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 Reference 442

Magnetic pulse welding discharges a large stored electrical charge through a coil placed around or beside a workpiece. The restriction of lead in electronics and in potable water plumbing changed the process substantially, and the changes are worth stating because they explain much of modern soldering practice:

• Narrower process windows. The gap between "hot enough to wet properly" and "hot enough to damage the component" narrowed.

5. Hydrogen Porosity: The Characteristic Aluminium Defect

Hydrogen is highly soluble in molten aluminium and almost insoluble in solid aluminium. During solidification the dissolved hydrogen is rejected from the advancing solid, becomes supersaturated in the remaining liquid, and forms bubbles. If the pool solidifies before the bubbles escape, they are trapped as porosity.

This mechanism is unavoidable in principle and controllable in practice. Sources of hydrogen:

• Moisture in the oxide film on the parent metal or on the filler wire — the largest single source in most shops.

• Hydrocarbons: oil, grease, cutting fluid, drawing lubricant residue on filler wire, fingerprints.

10. Reheat Cracking in Creep-Resistant Steels

Also called stress-relief cracking. It occurs during post-weld heat treatment or during high-temperature service, not during welding.

Mechanism. In creep-resistant steels containing strong carbide formers — chromium, molybdenum, vanadium, niobium — the coarse-grained heat-affected zone is left after welding with those elements in solution. On reheating to stress-relief temperature, fine carbides precipitate inside the grains, strengthening the grain interiors relative to the grain boundaries. Residual stress then relaxes preferentially by sliding at the weakened boundaries, and intergranular cracks form in the coarse-grained heat-affected zone.

QUESTION: Why does duplex stainless steel have both a heat-input ceiling and a floor?

Duplex stainless steel has both a heat-input ceiling and a floor to ensure that the weld metal achieves the required mechanical properties without causing excessive distortion or cracking. The heat-input ceiling prevents the weld from becoming too hot, which could lead to loss of ductility, while the heat-input floor ensures sufficient heat to achieve proper fusion and minimize residual stresses.
